title: Sunde, Managing the Unmanageable — legal culture as an analytical tool

slides.title: Why legal culture became a subject
slides.text: The book's opening thesis: CHANGES IN COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGY HAVE ENORMOUSLY INCREASED INTERACTION ACROSS GEOGRAPHICAL DISTANCES, and thereby created new kinds of social relations which need to be regulated by TRANSNATIONAL LAW — law valid ACROSS the boundaries of a nation state's jurisdiction and WITHIN it. LAW IS THEREFORE NO LONGER PREDOMINANTLY A NATIONAL AFFAIR, and without an understanding of different legal cultures our perception of the contemporary legal order will be incomplete. Norway has the figures for it: the first small step was in 1988, when the EEC directive on product liability was used as the model for a Norwegian statute — at that time AN ESTIMATED LESS THAN 1 PER CENT OF VALID NORWEGIAN LAW came from sources outside Norwegian jurisdiction. In 1994 the EEA AGREEMENT entered into force and made large parts of EU law part of Norwegian law; in 1999 the EUROPEAN CONVENTION ON HUMAN RIGHTS became part of it too; and a Supreme Court precedent of 2000 effectively placed Norway inside the transnational order. The indicator is eloquent: THE EUROPEAN COURT OF HUMAN RIGHTS DECIDED 25 CASES IN 1989 — THE YEAR THE BERLIN WALL FELL — 177 IN 1999, AND IN 2009 REACHED AN ALL-TIME HIGH OF 1,623 CASES.

cards.q: Why did the need to compare legal cultures arise?
cards.a: Because new communication technologies increased interaction across distances and created relations requiring TRANSNATIONAL LAW — valid across the boundaries of jurisdiction and within them. Law thereby ceased to be predominantly a national affair, and without an understanding of legal cultures our perception of the present order is incomplete.

cards.q: How quickly did Norway enter the transnational legal order?
cards.a: 1988, the first EEC directive used as a model statute, when less than 1 per cent of valid law came from foreign sources; 1994, the EEA Agreement made large parts of EU law Norwegian law; 1999, the same with the ECHR; and a Supreme Court precedent of 2000 completed it. The accompanying figure: the ECtHR decided 25 cases in 1989, 177 in 1999 and a record 1,623 in 2009.

slides.title: The map of Bergen: why we do not want a 1:1 map
slides.text: Sunde's central image, and it is worth being able to tell. On the cover of the book is a copperplate engraving of Bergen by ALAIN MANESSON MALLET, published in Paris in 1683 in the five volumes of the DESCRIPTION DE L'UNIVERS. Mallet was an engineer, an officer and a CARTOGRAPHER; HE HAD NEVER BEEN TO BERGEN HIMSELF and relied on very accurate descriptions. That is why the castle is too small in relation to the Rosenkrantz Tower and St Mary's church too large in relation to both — BUT ANYONE WHO STUDIES THAT MAP GAINS NOT ONLY A GOOD IMPRESSION OF THE CITY BUT CAN ALSO FIND HIS WAY FROM ONE PART OF IT TO ANOTHER, although it is not a street plan. And that is precisely the point about legal culture: TO MAP IT AND FIND ONE'S WAY IN IT. There is no limit to how many careful studies can be made before the map is drawn — just as there is no limit to how minutely the elements of a legal culture can be examined. BUT JUST AS A 1:1 MAP IS USELESS TO A TRAVELLER, SO A PRESENTATION OF A LEGAL CULTURE THAT CAREFULLY EXAMINES EVERY SHADE OF EVERY DETAIL IS USELESS TO A STUDENT OR A USER OF LAW. The aim is not an accurate representation of the world but A TOOL USABLE FOR ORIENTATION IN UNFAMILIAR TERRAIN — and the appropriate degree of detail is dictated by the PURPOSE.

cards.q: What does Sunde's image of the map of Bergen mean for the study of legal culture?
cards.a: That the aim is not an accurate representation of the world but A TOOL FOR ORIENTATION IN UNFAMILIAR TERRAIN, and that the degree of detail is dictated by the PURPOSE. Mallet had never been to Bergen and his proportions are wrong, yet one can walk from place to place by his map. And conversely: a 1:1 map is useless to a traveller, as is a description of a legal culture examining every shade of every detail.

slides.title: What it is supposed to be good for
slides.text: The purpose of legal culture as an analytical tool is TO MAKE DIFFERENT CONCEPTIONS OF LAW AND OF HOW LAW OPERATES IN SOCIETY INTELLIGIBLE TO THE EXTENT THAT THEY DO NOT FORM AN OBSTACLE TO COOPERATION. This holds for the lawyer advising a client, the judge deciding a case, the member of parliament voting on a statute, the official or politician in an international body preparing supranational legislation, and the scholar drafting a common frame of reference for the whole field. BUT THEY DO NOT WORK IN THE SAME TIME FRAME OR ON THE SAME SCALE OF CONSEQUENCES: from the lawyer to the scholar THE TIME AVAILABLE FOR INVESTIGATION BEFORE ACTING INCREASES DRAMATICALLY — AND SO DOES THE EFFECT OF THEIR LEGAL ACTS. That is a neat point: whoever has the least time does the least damage. Sunde compares it with legal philosophy: LEGAL PHILOSOPHY HAS ALREADY BEEN PUT INTO PRACTICE AS LEGAL METHODOLOGY, because every application of law cannot rest on a thorough analysis but on a REWORKED FORM IN THE SHAPE OF A METHOD. The same is to happen with legal culture — THE AIM IS TO GIVE THE READER TOOLS FOR MAKING LEGAL-CULTURAL KNOWLEDGE OPERATIVE IN THE EVERYDAY WORKING OF LAW.

cards.q: What is legal culture as an analytical tool supposed to achieve?
cards.a: To make different conceptions of law and of its operation in society intelligible to the extent that they DO NOT FORM AN OBSTACLE TO COOPERATION — for the lawyer, the judge, the legislator, the official in an international body and the scholar. Note also that from the lawyer to the scholar the time for investigation before acting increases, and so does the effect of their legal acts.

cards.q: How does Sunde compare legal culture with legal philosophy?
cards.a: Legal philosophy has already been put into practice as LEGAL METHODOLOGY — because every application of law cannot rest on a thorough analysis of it but on a reworked form. He wants to do the same with legal culture: to give tools for making legal-cultural knowledge OPERATIVE in the everyday working of law.

slides.title: The definition: what legal culture is
slides.text: An important admission: LEGAL CULTURE IS A LABEL WE PUT ON THE OBSERVATIONS WE MAKE. In Norway, for instance, there is only ONE COURT HIERARCHY with mostly general courts and judges who routinely decide civil, criminal, administrative and constitutional matters; specialised courts are few. Supreme Court decisions are regarded as BINDING IN EFFECT but HAVE NO FORMAL BINDING FORCE BEYOND THE CASE AT HAND, and decisions of lower courts not even that. At the same time THERE IS NO REAL CIVIL CODE IN NORWAY nor any other codes, but INDIVIDUAL STATUTES AND A GREAT MANY REGULATIONS, plus precedent and a range of further sources such as PREPARATORY WORKS, CUSTOM AND VALUE CONSIDERATIONS. And now the definition. We call observations of law legal culture BECAUSE THEY INFLUENCE HOW LAW OPERATES, and because they are as a rule governed by IDEAS SHARED AND EXPRESSED IN ACTION WITHOUT MUCH REFLECTION OR ANALYSIS. In this law resembles language and taste. BUT UNLIKE LANGUAGE AND TASTE, LAW IS AN INSTRUMENT OF GOVERNANCE, which ties it to POWER. The relation of law and power is twofold: LAW MAKES POWER MORE EFFECTIVE BECAUSE IT ALLOWS RULE WITHOUT PHYSICAL PRESENCE, AND AT THE SAME TIME LIMITS POWER, BECAUSE POWER NOT EXERCISED ACCORDING TO LAW APPEARS ILLEGITIMATE. Either way, the relation of law and power drives LAW TOWARDS INSTITUTIONALISATION, even in a society without a state. Hence the definition: LEGAL CULTURE IS IDEAS OF AND EXPECTATIONS TO LAW MADE OPERATIONAL BY INSTITUTIONAL (OR INSTITUTION-LIKE) PRACTICES.

terms.def: Ideas of and expectations to law, made operational by institutional (or institution-like) practices.

cards.q: How does Sunde define legal culture?
cards.a: As IDEAS OF AND EXPECTATIONS TO LAW, MADE OPERATIONAL BY INSTITUTIONAL (OR INSTITUTION-LIKE) PRACTICES. It is a label on the observations we make — naming what influences how law operates and what is governed by shared ideas expressed in action without much reflection.

cards.q: How does law differ from language and taste as a cultural product?
cards.a: In being an INSTRUMENT OF GOVERNANCE, and therefore tied to POWER. The relation is twofold: law makes power more effective because it allows rule without physical presence, and at the same time limits it, because power not exercised according to law appears illegitimate. Both drive law towards INSTITUTIONALISATION, even in a stateless society.

slides.title: Why not 'system', 'tradition' or 'family'
slides.text: Sunde goes through the alternative names and rejects each for a specific reason — this is a typical exam question. LEGAL SYSTEM carries the connotation of A DELIBERATE CONSTRUCTION OF LAW THROUGH INSTITUTIONS, and therefore does not direct attention to the role of SHARED AND MORE OR LESS UNCONSCIOUS IDEAS; a purely institutional approach will not explain, for instance, WHY THERE IS ALMOST NO SPECIALISATION IN THE NORWEGIAN COURTS. LEGAL TRADITION has the opposite defect: IT PULLS ATTENTION TOWARDS IDEAS AND AWAY FROM SHARED INSTITUTIONS — an analysis of ideas about law will not fully explain why a whole range of sources including preparatory works and precedent is regarded as relevant in Norwegian law. The most relevant alternative is LEGAL FAMILY, a favourite concept of comparative law with connotations neither to ideas nor to institutions. But LEGAL FAMILY SUGGESTS A HIERARCHY WITH AN ORIGIN AND OFFSHOOTS AND DOES NOT REFLECT THE COMPLEX REALITY OF INFLUENCE AND DIALOGUE. Norway is the illustration: a long, settled and highly valued tradition of EXTENSIVE LEGISLATION in the continental spirit goes hand in hand with an equally long and valued tradition of THE EXTENSIVE USE OF PRECEDENT in the English spirit. WHICHEVER LEGAL FAMILY YOU PUT NORWEGIAN LAW IN, IT BECOMES THE BLACK SHEEP — and since this is more or less a feature of many small jurisdictions, putting them all into one family, into the 'ORPHANAGE OF COMPARATIVE LAW', has no clarifying effect at all.

cards.q: Why does Sunde reject the terms 'legal system' and 'legal tradition'?
cards.a: Legal SYSTEM connotes a deliberate construction of law through institutions and does not direct attention to shared, more or less unconscious ideas — a purely institutional view will not explain why there is no specialisation in the Norwegian courts. Legal TRADITION has the opposite defect: it pulls attention to ideas and away from shared institutions, so it will not explain why preparatory works and precedent count as sources of law.

cards.q: Why is 'legal family' not enough either? Show it on Norway.
cards.a: Because it suggests a HIERARCHY with an origin and offshoots and does not reflect the complexity of influence and dialogue. Norway has at once a long tradition of EXTENSIVE LEGISLATION in the continental spirit and of THE EXTENSIVE USE OF PRECEDENT in the English spirit — in any family it is therefore the black sheep. And herding all such small jurisdictions into one family, into the 'orphanage of comparative law', clarifies nothing.

slides.title: The sea of law: three layers
slides.text: A model taken from KAARLO TUORI (Critical Legal Positivism), inspired by the French ANNALES SCHOOL. Imagine law as a SEA DIVIDED INTO THREE LEVELS. ON THE SURFACE are ACTUAL, TIME-SPECIFIC LEGAL ACTS — a particular Supreme Court decision, say. AT THE MIDDLE LEVEL are the MORE ENDURING ASPECTS OF LAW — the idea, for instance, THAT PRECEDENT IS A SOURCE OF LAW. AT THE BOTTOM is the TREASURY OF LAW: FUNDAMENTAL IDEAS, such as THAT THERE ARE SOURCES OF LAW AT ALL. The analogy with language makes it vivid: on the surface WORDS, in the middle GRAMMAR, at the bottom THE TECHNOLOGY OF LANGUAGE (speech, the written document, the digital document). Words come and go like case law and statutory provisions; HOW WE INFLECT 'COMPUTER' CHANGES FAR LESS OFTEN — just as what counts as a source of law is far more stable than the content of the sources. And the Norwegian timeline: THE IDEA OF SOURCES OF LAW AROSE IN THE 13TH CENTURY, THE IDEA OF A WHOLE RANGE OF SOURCES IN THE 18TH, AND IN THE 21ST CENTURY THE IDEA OF SOURCES OF LAW IS BEING QUESTIONED.

terms.def: Tuori's layered model of law: on the surface concrete legal acts, in the middle more enduring ideas (precedent is a source), at the bottom fundamental ideas (that sources of law exist at all).

cards.q: Describe the three layers of the 'sea of law' and their linguistic analogue.
cards.a: On the surface concrete, time-specific legal acts (a court decision, a statutory provision) — in language, WORDS. In the middle more enduring ideas, such as that precedent is a source of law — in language, GRAMMAR. At the bottom fundamental ideas, such as that sources of law exist at all — in language, THE TECHNOLOGY OF LANGUAGE: speech, writing, the digital document.

slides.title: Why the layers settle the quarrel about whether culture is static
slides.text: Layering is not rocket science, but it is immensely important BECAUSE IT MAKES IT POSSIBLE TO HANDLE LEGAL-CULTURAL CHANGE. Culture is intuitively perceived as STATIC — a rock towering above the sea of change. And this is both true and untrue at once: LEGAL CULTURE IS STATIC AT THE VERY MOMENT AT WHICH IT IS DYNAMIC. Norwegian language and Norwegian law change constantly ON THE SURFACE, that is at the level of words and legal rules; far less often at the middle level; and at the bottom hardly ever. THIS MEANS THAT LEGAL CULTURE IS CONSTANTLY CHANGING AND AT THE SAME TIME RESTRAINING CHANGE — ONLY AT DIFFERENT LEVELS. And there is more: legal change is A MATTER OF COMPLEX INTERACTIONS BETWEEN THE LAYERS. Changes on the surface alter only some phenomena; but many constant and lasting changes can eventually alter the ideas at the middle level, and those in turn the ideas at the bottom. Movement can also go the other way, FROM THE TOP DOWN and FROM THE BOTTOM UP — but NEITHER DIRECTION IS EASY TO OBSERVE IN PURE FORM IN LEGAL HISTORY; they are SIMULTANEOUS MOVEMENTS. An illustration: the idea of written law does not appear to have begun either with the writing of ever more individual provisions or with the introduction of a written code, BUT WITH THE IDEA OF A WRITTEN CODE AND THE WRITING OF INDIVIDUAL PROVISIONS AND STATUTES AT ROUGHLY THE SAME TIME IN THE 12TH CENTURY. Legal-cultural change is therefore A DIALECTICAL MOVEMENT BETWEEN THE LAYERS. And what the model does NOT cover: THE IMPORTANT ROLE OF HISTORICAL EVENTS AND OF INDIVIDUAL ACTORS — the German experience of the Nazi regime, or the legal theorist TORSTEIN ECKHOFF in Norway.

cards.q: Is legal culture static or dynamic?
cards.a: Both at once, only at different levels: it changes constantly ON THE SURFACE (words, legal rules), far less often in the middle, and at the BOTTOM hardly ever. Legal culture is therefore constantly changing AND AT THE SAME TIME RESTRAINING CHANGE.

cards.q: Does legal change run from the top down or from the bottom up? Show it on written law.
cards.a: Neither direction is observable in pure form in history — they are SIMULTANEOUS, DIALECTICAL movements between the layers. The idea of written law began neither with the writing of individual provisions nor with the introduction of a code, but with THE IDEA OF A CODE AND THE WRITING OF INDIVIDUAL PROVISIONS AT ROUGHLY THE SAME TIME, in the 12th century.

cards.q: What does the model of the sea of law not capture?
cards.a: The role of HISTORICAL EVENTS AND INDIVIDUAL ACTORS in legal culture and its change — the German experience of the Nazi regime, or the legal theorist Torstein Eckhoff in Norway.

slides.title: Legal culture as a product of communication
slides.text: Briefly: LEGAL CULTURE IS CREATED AND MAINTAINED BY COMMUNICATION. The image: Mallet's map of Bergen shows few inhabitants. The city is on the one hand made up of individual burghers, on the other it is MUCH MORE THAN THEIR SUM — and that surplus is created by THE INTERPLAY BETWEEN THEM. The same holds of legal culture: it is made up of individual acts and ideas and is at the same time more than their sum. And this interplay creates A COMMUNITY IN IDEAS AND ACTION. Individual deviations and occasionally direct contradictions remain, but WHAT IS SHARED GROWS WITH THE DEGREE OF THAT INTERPLAY. Hence a sentence worth holding on to: LEGAL CULTURE IS NOT AN ENTITY THAT ERASES DIFFERENCES BUT ONE THAT CREATES COMMUNITY DESPITE DIFFERENCES — and its homogeneity depends on the degree of that interplay and on how far it succeeds in creating community.

cards.q: What creates legal culture according to Sunde, and what follows for differences within it?
cards.a: COMMUNICATION, that is the interplay of individual acts and ideas — legal culture is more than their sum. And the key consequence: IT IS NOT AN ENTITY THAT ERASES DIFFERENCES BUT ONE THAT CREATES COMMUNITY DESPITE DIFFERENCES; its homogeneity depends on the degree of that interplay.

slides.title: Bergen 1683: competing communication
slides.text: There is always COMPETING COMMUNICATION. In Bergen in 1683 there lived burghers of many nations — Mallet wrote: 'ITS INHABITANTS ARE NUMEROUS AND OF DIVERS NATIONS.' Into the mid-19th century it was said that ANYONE WHO WANTED TO TRADE IN BERGEN HAD TO MASTER SIX LANGUAGES BESIDES NORWEGIAN. Scots, English, French, Germans, Dutch, Danes and Norwegians all had their own languages, at home and in their communities. For a long time the most powerful were the GERMANS, because Bergen was ONE OF THE FOUR HANSEATIC KONTORS OUTSIDE THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE. And with law it was the same: EACH OF THOSE GROUPS PARTLY APPLIED ITS OWN COMMERCIAL RULES AMONG ITSELF, and each of the warehouses along the harbour had a NEIGHBOURHOOD COURT applying its own norms — but there was also a TOWN COURT for matters between members of different groups. A GERMAN MERCHANT AT THE HANSEATIC KONTOR WAS THEREFORE PART OF GERMAN AND NORWEGIAN LEGAL CULTURE AT ONCE. In the 16th century the communication structures of the Kontor were the most extensive and effective, so they influenced him most; IN THE 18TH CENTURY IT WAS THE OTHER WAY ROUND AND THE GERMAN MERCHANTS WERE SLOWLY DRAWN TOWARDS NORWEGIAN LEGAL CULTURE. This is not merely a historical situation: in today's Norway the SÁMI have their own legal culture because they have their own communication structures — and because of their nomadic way of life and long-undetermined borders they were also influenced by SWEDISH AND RUSSIAN legal culture. At the same time, with European integration through the Council of Europe and the EU, belonging to a EUROPEAN LEGAL CULTURE has grown for Norwegians and Sámi alike.

cards.q: How does Bergen in 1683 illustrate the coexistence of legal cultures?
cards.a: Each national group partly applied its own commercial rules among itself and each warehouse along the harbour had a NEIGHBOURHOOD COURT; for matters between groups there was a TOWN COURT. A German merchant at the Hanseatic Kontor was therefore part of German and Norwegian legal culture at once — and depending on whose communication structures were the more effective, the Kontor's influence prevailed in the 16th century and the Norwegian in the 18th.

slides.title: The basic unit is NOT the national legal culture
slides.text: From the foregoing one might infer that the basic legal-cultural unit is the NATIONAL legal culture. IT IS NOT — and Sunde refutes it retrospectively: to say that the German merchant in Bergen had to relate to German and Norwegian legal culture IS A BACKWARD-LOOKING VIEW, because IN 1683 NO UNIFIED GERMAN OR NORWEGIAN LEGAL CULTURE EXISTED. The Holy Roman Empire was divided into MORE THAN 300 JURISDICTIONAL UNITS, partly with their own norms and court hierarchies, and therefore partly with their own legal cultures. Norway had a unified law and court hierarchy from the Middle Ages, but their unity was SEVERELY WEAKENED IN THE 15TH CENTURY. IT IS THEREFORE MORE ACCURATE TO SAY THAT THE MERCHANT RELATED TO THE LEGAL CULTURE OF LÜBECK AND OF BERGEN. Only more than two centuries later did the nation develop as a political unit with strong and effective communication structures and become THE ABSOLUTELY DOMINANT LEGAL-CULTURAL UNIT IN EUROPE. Even so, the Sámi SURVIVED as a legal culture thanks to their own effective structures — and at the European level structures have arisen so effective that some see in them A THREAT TO NATIONAL LEGAL CULTURE.

cards.q: Is the national legal culture the basic unit? Does Sunde prove it by an example?
cards.a: It is not. In 1683 no unified German or Norwegian legal culture existed: the Holy Roman Empire was divided into more than 300 jurisdictional units and Norwegian unity had been severely weakened in the 15th century — one should properly speak of the legal culture of LÜBECK AND OF BERGEN. The nation prevailed as a legal-cultural unit only after two centuries of building effective communication structures.

slides.title: Dividing legal culture: four earlier proposals
slides.text: The trouble with the concept of legal culture is that it is sometimes used in a CONCEALING rather than a REVEALING way. If we ask why statutes and precedent have both been important sources in Norway for centuries, it can be 'explained' by saying that this is its legal culture. BUT THAT IS MERELY A LABEL ON THE UNKNOWN, WHICH EXPLAINS NOTHING IN ITSELF. To name a phenomenon legal culture is ONLY THE BEGINNING, NOT THE END. The necessary next step: TO ASK WHICH STRUCTURAL ELEMENTS OF THE LEGAL CULTURE MADE PRECEDENT AN IMPORTANT SOURCE. The tradition of dividing it is long and varied. FRANZ WIEACKER, 'Foundations of European Legal Culture' (lecture 1983, published 1985), examined 1) PERSONALISM, 2) LEGALISM, 3) INTELLECTUALISM. ZWEIGERT AND KÖTZ (1984/1992) defined 1) HISTORICAL BACKGROUND, 2) MODE OF THOUGHT, 3) INSTITUTIONS, 4) SOURCES OF LAW, 5) IDEOLOGY — as the elements constituting the STYLE OF A LEGAL FAMILY (not a culture). VAN HOECKE AND WARRINGTON (1999) worked with 1) THE CONCEPT OF LAW, 2) SOURCES, 3) LEGAL METHOD, 4) ARGUMENTATION, 5) LEGITIMATION, 6) IDEOLOGY. And CEES VAN DAMM (2009) examined 1) INDIVIDUALISM vs COLLECTIVISM, 2) MASCULINITY vs FEMININITY, 3) UNCERTAINTY AVOIDANCE, 4) POWER DISTANCE, 5) LONG-TERM vs SHORT-TERM ORIENTATION. And the conclusion, which is itself a methodological lesson: THERE IS NO CORRECT AND INCORRECT DIVISION, ONLY THE QUESTION OF WHAT SERVES THE PURPOSE — Wieacker was making a legal-historical survey, Zweigert and Kötz had a contemporary and more practical approach, van Hoecke and Warrington a scholarly one, and van Damm was aiming at differences in European tort law.

cards.q: Why is it not enough to say that something is 'due to legal culture'?
cards.a: Because that is MERELY A LABEL ON THE UNKNOWN which explains nothing in itself — the concept is then used in a concealing rather than a revealing way. To name a phenomenon legal culture is only the BEGINNING; the necessary next step is to ask WHICH STRUCTURAL ELEMENTS produced it.

cards.q: Is there a correct division of legal culture into elements?
cards.a: No — only the question of WHAT SERVES THE PURPOSE. Wieacker (personalism, legalism, intellectualism) was making a legal-historical survey; Zweigert and Kötz (historical background, mode of thought, institutions, sources, ideology) had a practical approach to the style of a legal FAMILY; van Hoecke and Warrington a scholarly one; van Damm (individualism vs collectivism and so on) was aiming at European tort law.

slides.title: Sunde's model: two structures, six elements
slides.text: THIS IS THE CORE OF THE WHOLE ARTICLE AND THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO REMEMBER. Sunde divides legal culture first into an INSTITUTIONAL and an INTELLECTUAL STRUCTURE and then into SIX STRUCTURAL ELEMENTS: 1) CONFLICT RESOLUTION, 2) NORM PRODUCTION, 3) THE IDEA OF JUSTICE, 4) LEGAL METHOD, 5) PROFESSIONALISATION, 6) INTERNATIONALISATION. Together they form the LEGAL-CULTURAL MODEL. The first two belong to the INSTITUTIONAL structure, the remaining four to the INTELLECTUAL one. Sunde admits two things about it: THE MODEL CANNOT CLAIM UNIVERSAL VALIDITY — and at the same time it has PROVED ITSELF IN SURPRISINGLY DIFFERENT CONTEXTS, not least because it is FLEXIBLE AS TO THE THOROUGHNESS of the investigation. Every article in the book is built on this model: that is why the chapters on England and Wales, Scotland, Austria, Estonia, Finland and China have the same sections.

terms.def: Two structures — institutional and intellectual — and six elements: conflict resolution, norm production, the idea of justice, legal method, professionalisation, internationalisation.

cards.q: Name the six structural elements of Sunde's legal-cultural model and their division into two structures.
cards.a: INSTITUTIONAL structure: 1) conflict resolution, 2) norm production. INTELLECTUAL structure: 3) the idea of justice, 4) legal method, 5) professionalisation, 6) internationalisation.

cards.q: Does Sunde's model claim universal validity?
cards.a: It does not — Sunde says so expressly. At the same time he claims it has proved itself in surprisingly different contexts, chiefly because it is FLEXIBLE as to the thoroughness of the investigation.

slides.title: The institutional structure: conflicts and norms
slides.text: The institutional structure consists of THE INSTITUTIONS IN WHICH LAW IS SHAPED BY VARIOUS PRACTICES. The most fundamental are those that RESOLVE CONFLICTS — simply because CONFLICT RESOLUTION IS THE MOST BASIC DEMAND A SOCIETY MAKES OF ITS LEGAL ORDER; it is by this that peace and security can prevail in a society. NORM PRODUCTION is an activity that has GRADUALLY, AT LEAST IN PART, BECOME INDEPENDENT of conflict resolution. That development is worth knowing in steps: ORIGINALLY LEGAL NORMS WERE PRODUCED BY DECIDING CASES — each time a conflict was resolved, a norm arose. In time those norms were REUSED IN SIMILAR CASES and CASE LAW appeared. Case law could then be SYSTEMATISED AND DEVELOPED BY A LEGISLATOR, who could go on to BEGIN LEGISLATING INDEPENDENTLY OF JUDICIAL PRACTICE and thereby create a new institutionalised practice within law. THE LAST STEP IS CODIFICATION. In this way legislation became the dominant method of norm production. BUT PRECEDENT HAS NOT BEEN SUPERSEDED BY LEGISLATION IN ALL LEGAL CULTURES and in most it still plays a role — AND THAT ROLE IS GROWING IN THE PERIOD OF THE INTERNATIONALISATION OF LAW, DRIVEN FORWARD BY TRANSNATIONAL COURTS AND THEIR CASE LAW.

cards.q: Describe the development of norm production from deciding cases to codification.
cards.a: Originally norms were produced by DECIDING CASES — every resolution of a conflict was a norm. These were then reused in similar cases and CASE LAW arose. Case law could be systematised by a LEGISLATOR, who then began legislating independently of judicial practice. The last step is CODIFICATION. Precedent, however, was not superseded everywhere — and its role grows with an internationalisation driven by transnational courts.

cards.q: Why is conflict resolution the most fundamental institution of a legal culture?
cards.a: Because CONFLICT RESOLUTION IS THE MOST BASIC DEMAND A SOCIETY MAKES OF ITS LEGAL ORDER — it is by this that peace and security can prevail. Norm production became independent of it only gradually and only in part.

slides.title: The intellectual structure: justice, method, profession, internationalisation
slides.text: The production and application of norms does not happen in an intellectual vacuum. The most fundamental element is the IDEA OF JUSTICE. Sunde sharpens it: CONFLICTS RESOLVED ARBITRARILY, BY LOT SAY, ARE BETTER THAN CONFLICTS LEFT UNRESOLVED — which is why lots were drawn in desperate situations. BUT SOLUTIONS EXPERIENCED AS JUST HAVE A FAR HIGHER DEGREE OF LEGITIMACY, and are therefore accepted more often and more widely. What counts as just IS NOT CONSTANT and differs from place to place, from time to time, AND MAY EVEN DIFFER BETWEEN BRANCHES OF LAW — yet there will always be some PREVAILING idea of justice. LEGAL METHOD is what MAKES THE IDEA OF JUSTICE OPERATIONAL: it is simply THE WAY IN WHICH IDEAS OF JUSTICE ARE TRANSFORMED FROM VALUES AND VARIOUS SOURCES INTO LEGAL RULES APPLIED TO DECIDE A PARTICULAR DISPUTE. Its further task is TO CREATE A FRAMEWORK TIGHT ENOUGH FOR AN OTHERWISE UNCERTAIN PASSAGE FROM LEGAL RAW MATERIAL TO A REFINED RULE, AND TO MAKE IT INTERSUBJECTIVE. PROFESSIONALISATION means two things: that those who administer law on society's behalf devote MORE AND MORE OF THEIR TIME to it, and that there are SPECIAL CRITERIA THEY MUST MEET before law is entrusted to them. And all kinds of professionalisation have THE SAME EFFECT: THEY GIVE LAWYERS AN INTERNAL VIEW OF LAW — good law becomes, in the professional's eyes, increasingly a matter of INTERNAL COHERENCE, while for the non-professional it remains a matter of JUSTICE IN THE PARTICULAR CASE. INTERNATIONALISATION here refers to ALL KINDS OF INFLUENCE OF LEGAL MATERIAL PRODUCED OUTSIDE THE JURISDICTION. The reasoning: if society changes, law must change too; ONLY EXCEPTIONALLY CAN LAW BE CHANGED ON THE BASIS OF MERE EXPERIMENT, and reforms usually rest ON EXPERIENCE — and the main sources of experience are HISTORY AND COMPARATIVE LAW. The extensive use of comparative law in reform makes law A SOCIAL AND CULTURAL NOMAD.

cards.q: Why is it not enough to resolve a conflict arbitrarily, if even a lot is better than nothing?
cards.a: Because solutions experienced as JUST have a far higher degree of LEGITIMACY, and are therefore accepted more often and more widely. The lot was a device of desperate situations. What counts as just is not constant — it differs by place, time and branch of law, but some idea always prevails.

cards.q: What is legal method and what are its two tasks?
cards.a: The way in which ideas of justice are TRANSFORMED FROM VALUES AND SOURCES OF LAW INTO RULES applied to decide a particular dispute. Its second task is to create a FRAMEWORK TIGHT ENOUGH for the otherwise uncertain passage from legal raw material to a refined rule, and to make it INTERSUBJECTIVE.

cards.q: What effect does professionalisation have on what counts as good law?
cards.a: All kinds of professionalisation give lawyers an INTERNAL VIEW OF LAW: good law becomes for the professional increasingly a matter of INTERNAL COHERENCE, while for the non-professional it remains a matter of JUSTICE IN THE PARTICULAR CASE.

cards.q: Why does Sunde say that law is a 'social and cultural nomad'?
cards.a: Because if society changes law must change, and it can only exceptionally be changed by mere experiment — reforms rest on EXPERIENCE, whose main sources are HISTORY AND COMPARATIVE LAW. The extensive use of comparative law in reform therefore keeps moving law across borders.

slides.title: The model in action: why precedent is a source of law in Norway
slides.text: An illustration of how the model answers a question that could otherwise only be 'labelled'. CONFLICT RESOLUTION: Norway has ONE court hierarchy with almost no specialised courts at any level — that is, almost a PYRAMID with the Supreme Court at the apex, able to TRANSMIT PRECEDENT TO ALL THE LOWER COURTS. NORM PRODUCTION: Norway is governed by some 700 STATUTES AND 10,000 REGULATIONS but by NO CODE; efforts at harmonisation exist, but WITHOUT THE SYSTEM OF LAW THAT A CONTINENTAL CODIFICATION PROVIDES, STATUTORY LAW NEEDS ANOTHER UNIFYING FORCE — and that role is played by the Supreme Court through its precedent. THE IDEA OF JUSTICE: this is possible because justice is not strict predictability but the idea THAT LAW SHOULD BE ADAPTED IN APPLICATION SO AS TO GIVE A DECENT RESULT IN THE INDIVIDUAL CASE — and the instrument that keeps this practice from becoming arbitrary is precisely Supreme Court precedent, which unifies the adaptation. LEGAL METHOD is therefore NOT STRICTLY DEDUCTIVE but uses A RANGE OF SOURCES, so that application is flexible without being arbitrary. PROFESSIONALISATION: it helps that LAY JUDGES still play a significant role in criminal matters (much less in civil ones today) and that Norwegian legal scholarship HAS NOT SOUGHT TO CREATE A SYSTEM OF LAW that would replace the role of precedent. INTERNATIONALISATION, especially in human rights, has been PARTLY DRIVEN BY THE COURTS, with the Supreme Court leading the unification of norms produced inside and outside Norwegian jurisdiction.

cards.q: Why is precedent a source of law in Norway? Answer through the model.
cards.a: Conflict resolution: one almost pyramidal hierarchy without specialisation, so the Supreme Court can transmit precedent to all. Norm production: some 700 statutes and 10,000 regulations but NO CODE — statutory law needs another unifying force. The idea of justice: not strict predictability but adaptation of law for a decent result, which precedent unifies. Method: not deductive but drawing on a range of sources. Professionalisation: lay judges, and a scholarship with no ambition to build a system. Internationalisation: driven by the courts.

slides.title: Three caveats about the model — and internal versus external legal culture
slides.text: Sunde closes with three warnings. FIRST: NOT ALL STRUCTURAL ELEMENTS ARE RELEVANT TO ANSWERING A GIVEN QUESTION. SECOND: THERE MAY BE FURTHER ELEMENTS NOT PRESENT IN THE SIMPLIFIED MODEL — one could add LEGAL EDUCATION to the institutional structure (in Norway it certainly includes precedent) and LEGAL IDEOLOGY to the intellectual one (in Norway LEGAL REALISM, which elevates the adaptation of law by practice into an ideal). THIRD, and this is the most important caveat: THE MODEL CONCERNS ONLY THE INTERNAL LEGAL CULTURE, THAT IS, THE ONE SHARED BY PEOPLE WORKING WITH LAW. THE EXTERNAL LEGAL CULTURE, comprising ALL THOSE SUBJECT to a given legal culture, IS MUCH BROADER AND CANNOT BE FITTED INTO THE MODEL — it includes factors such as THE ECONOMY AND RELIGION, which may be relevant to legal culture but ARE NOT LEGAL IN NATURE. The relation of the two is like the relation of the map of Bergen on the front of the book to the map of Europe on the back: BERGEN IS BUT A TINY DOT IN EUROPE, JUST AS THE INTERNAL LEGAL CULTURE IS BUT A TINY DOT IN THE GENERAL CULTURE OF A SOCIETY. And yet — IF YOU ARE GOING TO BERGEN, YOU NEED A MAP OF BERGEN.

terms.def: The internal is shared by those working with law and is what the model covers. The external comprises all those subject to the culture, is much broader and includes the economy and religion — it does not fit into the model.

cards.q: What is the difference between internal and external legal culture?
cards.a: The INTERNAL is the one shared by people working with law — only that is covered by the model. The EXTERNAL comprises all those subject to the legal culture, is much broader and cannot be fitted into the model; it includes factors such as the economy and religion, which may be relevant but are not legal in nature.

cards.q: Which elements could still be added to the model?
cards.a: LEGAL EDUCATION to the institutional structure (in Norway it includes precedent) and LEGAL IDEOLOGY to the intellectual one — in Norway legal realism, which makes an ideal of adapting law through practice. The model is a simplification, not a closed list.
